The Greenspotted rockfish (Sebastes chlorostictus) attains a maximum total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of the genus Sebastes. This ultimate length is typically reached only after several decades of growth, reflecting the species' slow life-history pace. The estimated wet weight of a fully grown individual, derived from length-weight relationships, is approximately 1800 grams [Wwi = approximately 1800 grams], a mass consistent with the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of many rockfishes. Juveniles recruit to benthic habitats along the continental slope, where they feed on small crustaceans and begin a protracted period of somatic development. Field surveys indicate that individuals do not approach this asymptotic size until late in life, and the length composition of commercial trawl bycatch suggests that the largest specimens are predominantly female, a pattern common among iteroparous scorpaenids with determinate growth. The length at which 50 percent of the population is reproductively mature has been estimated at 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters] total length, corresponding to a wet body mass of roughly 161 grams [Wwp = roughly 161 grams] at the onset of puberty.

Reproductive output in Greenspotted rockfish has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions in laboratory mesocosms. At a stable temperature of 9.7 °C [T = 9.7 °C], females exhibit a maximum annual reproductive rate that can be decomposed into per-event fecundity of approximately 760,000 larvae per parturition [N_R_i = approximately 760,000 larvae per parturition], with typically one parturition per year [F_R_i = one parturition per year]. This species is viviparous, and the larval wet weight at birth is exceedingly small, measuring just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a mass that reflects the 0.8 millimeter diameter of the ova prior to fertilization. Such diminutive neonates are typical of rockfishes that produce large numbers of pelagic offspring as a bet-hedging strategy against high early-life mortality. The reproductive output is notably high for a fish of this body size, though it is achieved through the production of many small larvae rather than a few well-provisioned young. Comparative studies with other Sebastes species indicate that this combination of small birth size and elevated fecundity is associated with a prolonged larval pelagic duration and broad dispersal potential.

Lifespan data for Sebastes chlorostictus indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 12045 days [am = approximately 12045 days] when maintained at 9.7 °C [T = 9.7 °C], which translates to roughly 33 years of age. This extraordinary longevity is among the highest recorded for any teleost of this body size and is consistent with the slow growth, late maturity, and low natural mortality that characterize many deep-dwelling rockfishes. Age determination from otolith microstructure reveals that the oldest specimens are often those collected from deeper, colder portions of the species' depth range, suggesting that thermal environment plays a role in modulating senescence rates. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild may be even longer than captive estimates, as field-caught individuals occasionally exhibit annuli counts exceeding 35 years. This extreme life span, coupled with delayed maturity and low fecundity per reproductive bout relative to body mass, places the Greenspotted rockfish firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum for marine fishes. The ecological implications of such longevity include a low replacement rate and high vulnerability to overexploitation.

The length at puberty of 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters] represents a critical life-history transition at which energy allocation shifts from predominantly somatic growth toward gametogenesis and reproductive investment. This milestone is reached after several years of juvenile development, during which individuals accumulate sufficient lipid reserves in the liver and musculature to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and gestation. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental stage is 161 grams [Wwp = 161 grams], a body mass that appears to be a threshold below which successful parturition is rarely observed in gravid females. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across a latitudinal gradient shows that the onset of puberty is fairly consistent, with minimal geographic variation in the length or age at first maturation. This uniformity suggests strong genetic canalization of the maturation schedule, possibly as an adaptation to the relatively stable thermal regime of the continental slope environment. The ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] represents the upper bound of somatic growth, after which further increases in body size are negligible and energy is directed almost entirely toward annual reproductive bouts.

Comparisons among Sebastes species reveal that the maximum wet body weight of approximately 1800 grams [Wwi = approximately 1800 grams] in Greenspotted rockfish is intermediate relative to larger congeners such as Sebastes ruberrimus, which can exceed 7000 grams, and smaller species like Sebastes elongatus, which rarely surpass 500 grams. The larval wet weight at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] is among the smallest recorded for any viviparous teleost, rivaling the minute neonates of pelagic spawning fishes despite the constraints of internal gestation. This extreme reduction in offspring size is offset by the very high number of larvae produced per annual reproductive cycle, which at 9.7 °C [T = 9.7 °C] reaches approximately 760,000 larvae per parturition [N_R_i = approximately 760,000 larvae per parturition], a value that underscores the species' reliance on high fecundity rather than parental care. The long lifespan of 12045 days [am = 12045 days] at this same temperature regime allows many reproductive opportunities across a female's lifetime, contributing to a life-history strategy that buffers against sporadic recruitment failures at a temperature of 9.7 °C [T = 9.7 °C]. These demographic parameters collectively position Sebastes chlorostictus as a classic K-selected species, with delayed maturation, slow growth, great longevity, and iteroparous reproduction, all of which render it particularly sensitive to adult mortality from fishing pressure.
